result: TRPV4 channels are expressed in brain capillary endothelial cells (cECs) but exhibit very low basal activity. GSK101 (100 nM) failed to evoke detectable TRPV4 currents in perforated or conventional whole-cell recordings with 1 mM Mg-ATP, but breaking through from perforated patch or omitting Mg-ATP from the pipette solution resulted in robust TRPV4 currents that were abolished by HC-067047 and absent in TRPV4-/- mice.
evaluation: Claims C3, C29-C32, C36-C37, C39-C40 collectively demonstrate TRPV4 expression in cECs through pharmacological (GSK101 activation, HC-067047 blockade) and genetic (TRPV4-/- mice) validation. The differential responses under different recording conditions (perforated vs. conventional, with/without ATP) provide converging evidence for TRPV4 presence and its regulation.

result: Intracellular Mg-ATP (1 mM) dramatically suppresses TRPV4 channel activity in cECs. The EC50 for GSK101 shifted ~23-fold from 18 nM (without ATP) to 415 nM (with 1 mM Mg-ATP). Single-channel recordings showed that removing ATP increased channel open probability ~6-fold (from NPO=0.038 to 0.209), with basal open probability estimated at ~0.0002. This suppression was specific to adenosine nucleotides.
evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C38, C41-C47 provide comprehensive dose-response, single-channel, and nucleotide specificity data demonstrating ATP-dependent TRPV4 suppression. The convergence of whole-cell and single-channel measurements, along with nucleotide specificity controls (GTP had no effect), strongly supports this conclusion.

result: TRPV4 suppression by ATP requires ATP hydrolysis and Mg2+ but is independent of protein kinases A, G, and C. The non-hydrolyzable analog ATP-γ-S (1 mM) failed to inhibit TRPV4, and replacing Mg-ATP with Na-ATP (without Mg2+) abolished suppression. Inhibitors of PKA (H-89), PKG (KT5823), and PKC (calphostin C) had no effect, and lower ATP concentrations (10-100 μM) that activate most protein kinases failed to inhibit TRPV4.
evaluation: Claims C48-C54 systematically rule out protein kinase involvement through multiple complementary approaches: non-hydrolyzable ATP analog, Mg2+ requirement, specific kinase inhibitors, and concentration-dependence studies. The data consistently point away from protein kinase mechanisms and toward an ATP-hydrolysis-dependent process requiring millimolar concentrations.

result: PIP2 mediates ATP-dependent TRPV4 suppression in cECs. Four structurally unrelated PI4K inhibitors (wortmannin 50 μM, PIK93 300 nM, PAO 30 μM, LY294002 300 μM) reversed TRPV4 inhibition by ATP, while lower concentrations insufficient to inhibit PI4K had no effect. Direct application of PIP2 analogs (diC8-PIP2, diC16-PIP2) inhibited TRPV4 currents by 70-80%, and scavenging PIP2 with poly-L-lysine attenuated ATP effects.
evaluation: Claims C55-C64 provide multiple lines of evidence linking PIP2 to TRPV4 suppression: pharmacological inhibition of PIP2 synthesis (with appropriate concentration controls), direct PIP2 application, and PIP2 scavenging. The use of structurally unrelated PI4K inhibitors and multiple PIP2 analogs strengthens the conclusion.

result: PGE2 activates TRPV4 channels in cECs through EP1 receptor-mediated PIP2 depletion, independent of PIP2 metabolites DAG and IP3. PGE2 (2 μM) increased TRPV4 single-channel NPO ~6-fold and enhanced whole-cell currents in the presence of Mg-ATP. This effect was blocked by EP1 antagonists (AH6809, SC51322), PLC inhibitor U73122, and exogenous PIP2, but not by PKC inhibitors (Gö6976, calphostin C) or Ca2+ chelation (BAPTA, CPA).
evaluation: Claims C65-C79 systematically dissect the PGE2 signaling pathway using receptor antagonists, PLC inhibitors, exogenous PIP2, and inhibitors/chelators of downstream pathways. The convergence of single-channel and whole-cell data, along with appropriate pharmacological controls (inactive analog U73343), strongly supports the EP1-PLC-PIP2 depletion mechanism independent of DAG/IP3.

result: GqPCR-mediated TRPV4 activation is not universal across all GqPCR agonists. Carbachol (10 μM, muscarinic receptor agonist) induced TRPV4 currents comparable to PGE2, but ATP (50 μM, purinergic receptor agonist) and SLIGRL-NH2 (5 μM, PAR2 agonist) had no effect on TRPV4 activity.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 demonstrate differential effects of GqPCR agonists on TRPV4 activation. While carbachol mimics PGE2 effects, ATP and SLIGRL-NH2 do not activate TRPV4 despite their known GqPCR signaling capabilities. This selectivity is well-documented experimentally but the mechanistic basis remains unclear (as authors acknowledge).

result: PGE2 simultaneously enhances TRPV4 currents and inhibits Kir2.1 currents in cECs with comparable kinetics. Using perforated-patch recordings with 60 mM extracellular K+ and 2 μM GSK101, PGE2 (2 μM) rapidly (<60 s onset) increased TRPV4 currents and decreased Kir2.1 currents with similar time constants (τ=4.9 min for TRPV4, 6.4 min for Kir2.1). Carbachol produced similar bidirectional effects, while ATP inhibited Kir2.1 without affecting TRPV4.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 demonstrate bidirectional regulation through simultaneous monitoring of both channel types under physiological conditions (perforated patch). The kinetic analysis (C85) and comparison with time controls strengthen the conclusion. The differential effects of ATP (Kir2.1 inhibition only) provide an important control showing the effects are dissociable.

result: PIP2 functions as a master regulator that exerts opposite effects on TRPV4 (inhibition) and Kir2.1 (activation) channels in brain cECs, with GqPCR activation serving as a molecular switch. Under basal conditions, PIP2 tonically inhibits TRPV4 and supports Kir2.1 activity. GqPCR activation depletes PIP2, simultaneously disinhibiting TRPV4 and suppressing Kir2.1, thereby shifting the balance from hyperpolarizing (Kir2.1-mediated) to depolarizing (TRPV4-mediated) signaling.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C24-C26, C102, C117-C120 synthesize the major findings into a unified model. This conclusion is well-supported by the convergence of multiple experimental approaches: pharmacological manipulation of PIP2 levels, direct PIP2 application, simultaneous monitoring of both channel types, and demonstration of bidirectional regulation by GqPCR agonists. The model is internally consistent with all presented data.

result: Quantitative analysis suggests GqPCR activation produces sufficient TRPV4 current to functionally oppose K+-induced hyperpolarization. At physiological membrane potential (-40 mV), basal TRPV4 current is ~-80 fA while Kir2.1 current with 3 mM K+ is ~6 fA (increasing to ~260 fA with 10 mM K+). GqPCR activation increases TRPV4 open probability ~6-fold, producing 400-500 fA inward current sufficient to short-circuit K+-induced hyperpolarization.
evaluation: Claims C103-C107 present quantitative estimates based on calculations from experimental data and known channel properties. While the calculations appear reasonable, they rely on multiple assumptions and extrapolations from measured values at different voltages. The functional prediction (short-circuiting K+-induced hyperpolarization) is plausible but not directly tested experimentally in the manuscript.

result: The authors propose that TRPV4-mediated depolarization in cECs (which lack Ca2+-activated K+ channels) would lead to membrane depolarization rather than hyperpolarization, and that GqPCR-induced Ca2+ signals may serve dual roles: promoting vasodilation through NO release and acting as 'stop signs' to redirect electrical signals.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91, C108-C111 represent speculative interpretations about functional consequences. While C90-C91 are reasonable inferences based on the absence of Ca2+-activated K+ channels, C108-C111 are explicitly speculative (using terms like 'should,' 'presumably,' 'might,' 'may'). These hypotheses are plausible but lack direct experimental validation in the current manuscript.

result: The authors propose that brain cECs have a higher PIP2 'set point' compared to peripheral ECs, potentially due to lower GqPCR expression or higher PIP2 synthesis capacity. This higher PIP2 level would be necessary to saturate Kir2.1 channels and suppress TRPV4 sufficiently to prevent inappropriate membrane depolarization.
evaluation: Claims C112-C116 present speculative interpretations about PIP2 regulation in cECs. While C115-C116 cite transcriptomic and metabolic data from other studies, the proposed 'set point' difference is inferred rather than directly measured. The functional necessity argument (C113-C114) is logical but not experimentally validated in this manuscript.

result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about Kir2.1 channels in cECs, their role in neurovascular coupling, regulation by PIP2, and the absence of IK/SK channels in brain cECs. Also establishes that TRPV4 is regulated by PIP2 in other systems and is important in arterial/arteriolar ECs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C9, C13-C23, C27-C28 are background claims supported by citations to previous work, including the authors' own studies. These establish the context for the current investigation and are appropriately referenced.

result: General knowledge claims about GqPCR signaling, PIP2 metabolism, ion channel regulation, and previous findings on TRPV4 regulation by PIP2 in heterologous systems.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C55, C88-C89, C92-C96, C99-C101 represent established scientific knowledge or findings from previous studies, appropriately cited. These provide necessary background for interpreting the current results.

result: 11,12-EET (1 μM) evoked TRPV4 currents in cECs even without dialyzed PIP2, and the current results are the first to report PIP2-mediated suppression of TRPV4 in native endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), showing that 11,12-EET can activate TRPV4 independently of PIP2 manipulation. Claim C98 accurately characterizes the novelty of the findings in native cells, though it acknowledges congruence with one previous heterologous expression study (Takahashi et al., 2014).
